name: Freedom trash can protest

card.summary: A 1968 feminist protest in which women discarded bras, makeup and other beauty items into a trash can, a landmark in debate about beauty standards.

quick.overview:
On September 7, 1968, New York Radical Women and allies protested the Miss America pageant in Atlantic City. On the boardwalk they tossed items they saw as symbols of female oppression, such as bras, girdles, false eyelashes, high heels, curlers and makeup, into a 'Freedom Trash Can'.

It matters to appearance culture as a historic statement about beauty standards: protesters objected to the pageant's emphasis on youth, bodies and a narrow ideal. It is documented history rather than a method for improving looks.
quick.how: Protesters wore signs, paraded a sheep crowned 'Miss America', and dropped items into the can; four women unfurled a Women's Liberation banner inside the hall. The event is used in discussions of how grooming norms are questioned.
quick.risks: No health risks. Participants said no bras were burned, though a later historian found reports that some items were briefly set alight; the 'bra-burning' label is widely discussed.

lead: The Freedom Trash Can was the centerpiece of the September 7, 1968 protest of the Miss America pageant in Atlantic City, organized by New York Radical Women with Robin Morgan as a key organizer, alongside Kathie Sarachild and Carol Hanisch.[1]

Protesters threw bras, girdles, corsets, false eyelashes, high heels, curlers, hairspray, makeup, mops and copies of Cosmopolitan and Playboy into the can, and paraded a live sheep as Miss America to compare the pageant to livestock judging.[1]

For appearance culture the event records an early, high-profile challenge to the beauty ideals the pageant promoted, which participants described as focused on youth, commercialism and a narrow standard.[1]

angle.text: The protest is a historical reference point rather than a technique: it records people publicly rejecting the grooming items of the day, and it informs how people think about the norms they choose to follow or not.

paras: Men were barred from the action. Four protesters bought tickets and unfurled a 'Women's Liberation' banner during the outgoing Miss America's farewell speech and were quickly removed by police.[1] Morgan wrote the pamphlet No More Miss America! criticizing the pageant's ties to consumerism and militarism.[1]

Lindsy Van Gelder's New York Post story, 'Bra Burners and Miss America', compared the event to draft-card burning, and the label stuck. Participants said no bras were burned; historian Joseph Campbell later cited an Atlantic City Press report and a witness suggesting some items were briefly set on fire. Scholars such as Bonnie Dow argue opponents helped keep the image alive to trivialize the movement.[1]
The same day a separate protest crowned the first Miss Black America, Saundra Williams, objecting to the exclusion of Black women from Miss America rather than to beauty contests as such.[1]
